Neonatal Sonora mud turtles emerge from their leathery-shelled eggs after a period of embryonic development, and at the moment of hatching, these young individuals possess a carapace length of 2.7 centimeters [Lb = 2.7 centimeters] and a corresponding wet weight of 3.8 grams [Wwb = 3.8 grams], a value derived from studies on the congeneric narrow-bridged musk turtle Claudius angustatus. This modest size at emergence is typical of kinosternids, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritizes the production of multiple, relatively small offspring over fewer, larger neonates. The progression from the yolk-dependent embryo to an actively foraging hatchling marks a critical transition, as the young turtle must commence first exogenous feeding to support its rapid growth during the initial months of life. Field data indicate that after the egg hatching event, these juveniles exhibit a period of accelerated growth, gradually increasing in both carapace length and body mass as they navigate the challenges of predation and resource acquisition in their aquatic habitats.

As females mature, they undergo considerable somatic growth, ultimately attaining an adult carapace length that can reach 14.2 centimeters [Li = 14.2 centimeters] and an ultimate wet weight of 676 grams [Wwi = 676 grams] in the largest individuals. Males, by contrast, achieve a smaller maximum size, with an ultimate carapace length of 12.1 centimeters [Li = 12.1 centimeters] for males, a pattern of sexual dimorphism that is common among kinosternid turtles where females require larger body cavities to accommodate egg production. These asymptotic dimensions represent the culmination of the juvenile growth phase, after which individuals transition into the reproductively active adult stage. Growth rates in this species are strongly modulated by environmental temperature, with individuals in warmer, more productive waters reaching these ultimate sizes more rapidly than those inhabiting cooler, less productive desert streams. The difference in body size between the sexes is not merely a morphological curiosity but has direct implications for reproductive output, as larger females can produce larger clutches and thus contribute more significantly to population recruitment.

Sexual maturation in female Sonora mud turtles is initiated when they reach a carapace length of 10 centimeters [Lp = 10 centimeters], marking the onset of gonadal activation and the ability to produce their first egg clutch. Males, in contrast, reach puberty at a smaller body size, with a carapace length of 8.5 centimeters [Lp = 8.5 centimeters] at puberty for males, a discrepancy that allows males to begin participating in reproductive activities earlier than females. This threshold for reproductive maturity is not merely a function of age but is tightly linked to the attainment of a critical body size, ensuring that individuals have accumulated sufficient energy reserves to support the high metabolic demands of reproduction. The physiological transition from an immature organism to a breeding individual involves the maturation of the gonads and the onset of gametogenesis, processes that are influenced by both endogenous hormonal cues and external environmental factors such as temperature and photoperiod. Following this milestone, individuals are classified as post-pubertal adults and may begin engaging in cloacal copulation and subsequent nesting activities within their home range.

The maximum reproductive rate for this species has been estimated under controlled thermal conditions, with a water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C] yielding a total annual output of approximately 6 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 6 eggs per year], a figure derived from the product of average clutch size and nesting frequency, which is consistent with the moderate fecundity observed in other kinosternid turtles. This annual reproductive output is derived from data on the narrow-bridged musk turtle Claudius angustatus, which produces 2.4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2.4 eggs per clutch] and completes 2.5 clutches per year [F_R_i = 2.5 clutches per year] under similar thermal regimes. The 22 °C [T = 22 °C] temperature appears to represent an optimal thermal window for reproductive activity, balancing the energetic costs of egg production and incubation with the benefits of multiple nesting events. Gravid females invest considerable resources into each clutch, depositing their eggs in shallow nests excavated in sandy or muddy substrates along the margins of perennial water bodies. The timing of these nesting events is often synchronized with seasonal rainfall patterns, which help maintain appropriate soil moisture levels for successful incubation and subsequent eclosion of the hatchlings.

Longevity data for the Sonora mud turtle, recorded under a stable thermal environment of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 36.5 years [am = approximately 36.5 years], reflecting a slow-paced life-history strategy characteristic of many freshwater turtle species. This extended lifespan allows individuals to reproduce across multiple breeding seasons, thereby compensating for the relatively high mortality rates experienced during the vulnerable hatchling and juvenile stages. The ability to persist for more than three decades highlights the importance of adult survival as a key demographic parameter in this species, as even moderate annual mortality among breeding adults can significantly impact population stability. In their natural habitats, these turtles face a variety of threats including predation by raccoons, birds of prey, and large fish, as well as habitat degradation from agricultural runoff and water diversion. Conservation efforts for Kinosternon sonoriense must therefore prioritize the protection of both aquatic and terrestrial habitats to ensure that individuals can achieve their full lifespan and contribute to long-term population persistence across their range in the southwestern United States and northern Mexico.
